meta.ogDescription: Not Aristotle. Coined by religious scholar Marcus Bach in a 1954 graduation speech, per Quote Investigator; the Aristotle credit is a later invention.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — coined by Marcus Bach
answer.authorDates: 1901–1995 · American religious scholar & author, University of Iowa
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Aristotle ever wrote or said this. The line is documented in a 1954 high-school graduation speech by Dr. Marcus Bach of the State University of Iowa School of Religion, whom Quote Investigator ↗ provisionally credits as its originator. The Aristotle attribution first surfaced in the 1990s and repeats a secularized paraphrase (“Where your talents and the world’s needs cross, there lies your vocation”) that appears nowhere in Aristotle’s works.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: 1954 high-school graduation speech, reported in a newspaper

source.excerpt: the place where your talent meets the world’s needs is the job God has in mind for you
trail: 1954: Dr. Marcus Bach uses the line at a high-school graduation; it is the earliest documented appearance, per Quote Investigator ↗.
1957: a journalist, hearing Bach mention Albert Schweitzer in a speech, mistakenly credits the saying to Schweitzer — the first branch of misattribution, as QI documents ↗.

1993: a careers columnist attributes a secularized variant to Aristotle (“Where your talents and the world’s needs cross…”), later repeated in the 1997 book Zen Soup, as Quote Investigator ↗ documents — and scholars find no source in Aristotle, per Check Your Fact ↗.
Verdict: philosophy scholars confirm the line appears nowhere in Aristotle’s writings; QI provisionally credits Marcus Bach ↗.
source.excerptNote: The wording documented from Bach’s 1954 graduation address. His own 1971 book carried a close variant: “At that place in life where your talent meets the needs of the world, that is where God wants you to be.”

source.rightsNote: The exact wording is first documented in a 1954 speech and appears in Bach’s books from the mid-20th century onward — well after 1930 — so any published form is in copyright in the United States, held by the author’s estate and publishers. It is emphatically not an ancient, public-domain Aristotle text.

author.name: Marcus Bach
author.heading: Who was Marcus Bach?
author.bio: Marcus Bach (1901–1995) was an American religious scholar, dramatist and author who earned his Ph.D. from the University of Iowa’s interfaith School of Religion, where he was a professor from 1945 to 1964. A popular lecturer on world faiths and lesser-known religious movements, he wrote more than two dozen books, including Major Religions of the World and The Power of Perfect Liberty. His inspirational graduation lines circulated widely and were, over the decades, mis-credited to more famous names.

misattribution.heading: The misattribution trail
misattribution.intro: This is a modern inspirational line that has been pinned on two far more famous names. Neither said it.

items.why: There is no evidence Aristotle wrote or said this; philosophy scholars at Northwestern and Stanford confirmed to Check Your Fact ↗ that it appears nowhere in his works. The credit only surfaced in the 1990s.
A 1957 journalist wrongly credited Bach’s saying to Schweitzer after Bach mentioned him in a speech; the error was repeated in later books, as Quote Investigator ↗ traces.

misattribution.truthLine: The line was coined by religious scholar Marcus Bach, documented in a 1954 graduation speech, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why the mix-up stuck
lead: Aristotle’s ethics really do center on eudaimonia — flourishing through the exercise of one’s virtues — so a line about matching your talents to the world’s needs feels Aristotelian. That plausibility is exactly what let the false credit spread once a columnist attached his name to it in the 1990s.

But feeling Aristotelian is not the same as being Aristotle. The documented source is a 20th-century American religious scholar, and the “God has in mind” phrasing — theological, not classical — gives the real author away.
context.pull: A line about vocation and the divine plan, dressed up as ancient Greek philosophy.
